task.goal: Reduce intermittent USB printer disconnections at a community advice office without exposing documents.
hard_constraints: One shared computer and printer; no administrator rights, new hardware or cloud upload.
Test only blank or synthetic pages and do not inspect clients' document contents.
Separate cable, power, queue and software explanations using a reversible sequence during one after-hours session.
task.available_resources: Existing cable, outlet, print queue view and an empty test document.
task.expected_result: A bounded diagnosis and a practical fallback for the next opening day.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One-variable fault isolation with a bounded next-day fallback
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a 45–60 minute after-hours sequence to distinguish physical connection, power, queue and application explanations. The mechanism is controlled substitution of conditions: change one accessible factor, repeat the same synthetic job, and record only timing, printer indicators and queue status. This can identify a useful mitigation even if an intermittent fault cannot be reproduced reliably.

Prerequisites: permission to use the equipment after hours, an empty queue, and ordinary access to the printer controls and cable ends. Do not open queued documents, read job titles, cancel clients’ jobs or interrupt pending work. If the queue is occupied, defer disruptive steps and report that limitation. No administrator tools, downloads, replacement parts or cloud services are needed.

Start with three identical one-page synthetic jobs, submitted individually. Observe whether the printer loses power, remains powered but becomes unavailable, or stays available while jobs stall. Next, with the queue empty and equipment safely powered down, reseat only the existing USB cable and repeat. Then separately power down, reseat the accessible printer power connection at its existing outlet, restart and repeat. Do not manipulate damaged connectors or change electrical arrangements. For queue testing, compare individual submissions with a small batch of synthetic jobs; cancel only your own remaining jobs. For software testing, compare the same synthetic content through another already-installed printing application if available, keeping printer settings unchanged.

Restore ordinary settings and cable routing afterward. For opening day, use the successful condition only if supported: stable cable placement, one job at a time, or the working installed application. If disconnections persist, pause printing and arrange later collection through existing office procedures. Do not repeatedly resend sensitive jobs whose completion is uncertain.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Keep each stage to roughly five minutes and compare it with the unchanged baseline. A mitigation is weakened if the same failure recurs under it. Printer lights resetting supports a power explanation; continued power with lost availability supports a USB-path explanation; an available printer with stalled jobs supports queue/software investigation. These observations are clues, not proof: reseating and restarting can temporarily mask several faults. Where safe, repeat the baseline condition once; never deliberately loosen a connector. Record unresolved causes explicitly, especially if no failure occurs or no second application is available.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use the printer’s internal test as an independent diagnostic path
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a printer-generated test page to localize a failure while it is still present, before restarting or reseating anything. This bypasses the computer, application, queue and USB data path. The necessary assumption is that the printer has an ordinary button-operated self-test using built-in synthetic content. If that function is unavailable or requires changing persistent settings, this alternative cannot provide its main diagnostic advantage.

Bound the after-hours session to 45 minutes. Start only with an empty queue; if existing jobs are present, defer disruptive work without inspecting titles or contents. Use the existing computer, cable, outlet, printer controls and synthetic document. Record only elapsed time, power indicators, availability and synthetic-job progress.

First establish that an internal test and one computer-submitted synthetic page both print. Then alternate short idle intervals with individual synthetic submissions. If a submission fails, leave the connection and power unchanged and immediately request the internal test. An internal page that prints while the computer cannot reach the printer points toward the USB or host path. Lost power or a visibly restarting printer supports a power explanation. An illuminated printer that cannot produce its internal test leaves an internal printer fault unresolved; it does not establish a power fault.

Next, use the queue view to distinguish an unavailable device from an available device with stalled synthetic jobs. Cancel only your own jobs if ordinary permissions allow. Compare synthetic printing from a second already-installed application, if available, to assess application dependence. Finally, with the queue empty and printer switched off, reseat USB alone and retest; separately reseat the accessible power connection at the existing outlet and retest. Restore the original arrangement.

For opening day, adopt only a supported mitigation: stable cable placement, the working application, or individual submissions if batching caused stalls. If none is supported, use existing delayed-collection procedures and avoid repeated submissions of documents with uncertain completion.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: The smallest discriminating check is a failed computer submission immediately followed by a successful internal test, compared with their successful baseline pair. Repeat that pair once if time permits. This weakens a whole-printer power-loss explanation but cannot distinguish cable faults from host USB or driver faults. Conversely, failure of both paths weakens a purely application-specific explanation. Treat recovery after reseating as provisional because shutdown itself can clear faults. If no failure occurs, report the session as inconclusive; if no second application exists, leave application versus shared printing software unresolved.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Test an idle-triggered failure and use a controlled opening routine
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether disconnections depend on inactivity, then use a verified wake-and-check routine before client printing. The mechanism is to identify a transition into or out of an idle state as the trigger. This could support a practical workaround without changing drivers or protected power settings. It assumes ordinary access to printer controls, visible power indicators and the queue; an idle-related cause remains only a hypothesis.

Bound the after-hours session to 50 minutes. Begin only when the queue is empty, without reading existing job names or contents. Use a blank or synthetic one-page document. Record only elapsed time, indicators, device availability and the progress of your own jobs.

First compare two equal observation periods: submit a synthetic page every two minutes during one, and leave the equipment idle for ten minutes before submitting during the other. Keep cable placement, outlet, application and print settings fixed. Record whether the computer slept or the printer visibly entered standby. If failure follows idle, try the printer’s ordinary wake button once before another submission, without restarting or resending a possibly pending job.

Then separate competing explanations through reversible checks: with the queue empty and printer off, reseat USB alone and repeat the idle challenge; subsequently reseat the accessible power connection at the same outlet and repeat. Do not handle damaged connections. If the printer remains available but a synthetic job stalls, cancel only that job if permitted and compare a fresh submission. Compare another already-installed application if available; otherwise leave application versus shared printing software unresolved. Restore the original arrangement.

For opening day, use a synthetic preflight and the wake routine only if supported. If preflight fails, defer printing through existing office procedures. Never repeatedly submit client documents whose completion is uncertain.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: The smallest check compares the first page after ten minutes idle with a page after an equally long period of intermittent synthetic printing. Repeat the idle/wake comparison once if time permits. Failures during active printing weaken the idle-trigger hypothesis; a wake button that fails to restore printing weakens that workaround. Power-indicator resets, USB-only recovery and queue-only stalls provide separate clues, not definitive diagnoses. No reproduced failure means an inconclusive session, not proof of repair.

EXPAND.title: Test idle transitions and use a wake-before-print routine
EXPAND.proposal:
Target failures that occur when the computer or printer returns from an idle state. A timed wake-before-print routine could avoid a failed USB wake handshake without changing drivers or requiring administrator rights. This assumes the intermittent fault is related to idle time; that remains unproven.

One designated staff member runs a maximum 60-minute after-hours trial. Begin only when the queue is empty; if existing jobs are visible, do not inspect their titles or contents and defer disruptive work. Use the existing empty document, ordinary printer controls and queue status. Record only elapsed times, availability, power indicators and synthetic-job outcomes.

First submit a blank page while both devices are awake. Leave the equipment untouched for ten minutes, then submit another. Repeat the idle interval, but this time wake the computer and printer using their ordinary controls, wait for readiness, and then submit. Keep cable position and print settings unchanged. This changes the wake sequence rather than merely restarting equipment after failure.

Then separate competing explanations using brief, reversible checks: with an empty queue, reseat USB and repeat an awake submission; separately restart only the printer at its existing power connection and repeat; finally close and reopen the application with only the empty test document and repeat. Record whether failures track an idle transition, a cable intervention, a power reset, a persistent queue stall or an application session. These are competing clues, not definitive component diagnoses.

If waking first repeatedly helps, opening-day staff can use that routine before the first job after a quiet period. If it fails, stop resubmitting uncertain jobs and use the office’s existing deferred-printing procedure. Restore any ordinary settings changed during testing.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare direct submission after idle with wake-before-print after the same idle interval, ideally twice each within the time limit. Count completed blank pages, stalls and additional waiting time. Against the prior reseat-and-repeat route, this adds value only if failures follow idle transitions and the wake routine improves completion. Stop at 60 minutes, any client job arrival or abnormal power behavior. If neither condition fails, report the idle hypothesis as unresolved; do not claim a successful fix.

EXPAND.title: Test electrical interference by separating USB and power cable routes
EXPAND.proposal:
Target USB signal interference where the existing USB cable runs alongside a mains lead or power supply. Separating their routes could improve communication while retaining the same cable, ports and outlet. This is feasible only if existing slack allows safe separation without stretching cables, moving equipment precariously or obstructing access. It cannot establish that the cable itself is sound.

One staff member owns a 45-minute after-hours trial. Require an empty queue and use only blank pages. Avoid opening existing jobs or recording document names. Before changing anything, submit three individual blank pages and note printer power indicators, queue status and completion.

Safely power down, then reposition only the accessible middle section of the USB cable away from power leads and adapters. Leave both USB plugs seated and the printer’s power connection unchanged. Restore power and repeat the same submissions. For comparison, perform an equivalent power-down and restart with the original routing, provided that routing is safe. This controls partly for the restart itself. Never recreate a strained or damaged arrangement.

Use the remaining time for separate checks: reseat only USB with equipment safely off, test again, then separately reseat the accessible printer power connection at its existing outlet and test. With an empty queue, reopen the application containing the blank document and repeat once. Persistent stalls while the device remains available support queue or software investigation; power-indicator resets support a power explanation. Neither observation proves its cause.

Retain separated routing for opening day only if it is safe and supported by the trial. Restore other conditions and leave a short record of outcomes and uncertainties. If printing remains unreliable, defer documents through existing office procedures and hand the observations to whoever maintains the equipment.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare original and separated routing under matched restart and submission conditions. Record successful pages, disconnections and added setup time or cable strain. Relative to the prior cable-reseating route, separation must show improvement beyond an equivalent restart; otherwise its added work has no demonstrated benefit. A failure under separated routing weakens the hypothesis. Stop immediately for damaged insulation, unstable placement, client jobs or the 45-minute limit. If no fault reproduces, report an inconclusive test rather than attributing the issue to interference.

EXPAND.title: Controlled isolation with a recovery gate before reopening
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: the one-variable fault-isolation route, the strongest general route because it covers all four required explanations. Preserve its baseline, separate USB and power checks, queue comparison, installed-application comparison and rollback. Change the opening-day decision: a condition that completes fresh pages is usable only after checking that it leaves no synthetic job pending or liable to print later. This closes a recovery gap: apparent improvement can coexist with a stranded job and encourage duplicate submissions.

One designated staff member runs a maximum 60-minute after-hours session using the existing cable, outlet, queue view and blank document. Start only with an empty queue. Do not inspect client document contents or job titles, cancel client jobs, or change restricted settings. If existing work prevents an empty queue, defer disruptive testing and record the limitation.

Submit three individual blank pages, noting completion, elapsed time, device availability and power indicators. With an empty queue and equipment safely off, reseat only USB, restart and repeat. Separately reseat the accessible printer power connection at the same outlet and repeat under equivalent restart conditions. Compare individual synthetic submissions with a small batch for queue behavior. If another suitable application is already installed, compare the same blank content with unchanged print settings; otherwise mark application isolation incomplete. Power resets, powered-but-unavailable behavior and available-but-stalled jobs distinguish investigative branches, not proven causes.

After any failure, stop submissions. Cancel only your synthetic jobs using ordinary controls, and verify that the queue clears before another intervention. If cancellation remains stuck, end disruptive testing rather than stack further jobs or attempt administrator repairs. Restore safe cable routing and ordinary settings.

For opening day, the designated staff member leaves the successful procedure and unresolved limits for the staff member already responsible for printing. Until that person accepts the handoff, the tester remains responsible for confirming the queue is clear; an interrupted or uncleared session means printing stays deferred. Use a supported mitigation only provisionally. After any uncertain client print, stop resending and follow existing deferred-printing procedures without inspecting its contents. Compared with the source, this adds a short clearance check and may defer more printing, but reduces duplicate-output and abandoned-queue risk.
EXPAND.experiment: Reserve the final ten minutes of the 60-minute session for recovery and handoff. After the best-performing condition, submit two blank pages individually and confirm both physical output and an empty queue. If a synthetic job stalled earlier, assess whether ordinary cancellation actually cleared it before proceeding. A persistent stall, unexplained extra page, abnormal power behavior or arrival of client work ends the trial. Record only synthetic-job counts, timings and device/queue states. No reproduced fault means an inconclusive diagnosis; successful fresh pages alone do not establish safe recovery or a durable fix.

EXPAND.title: Idle-transition diagnosis with an explicit failed-wake exit
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: the wake-before-print route, a competitive low-burden mechanism when failures follow quiet periods. Preserve its awake baseline, matched idle comparisons, separate cable and power checks, application restart and rollback. Change the daily wake procedure by adding an exit before document submission: if ordinary waking does not produce readiness within a bounded interval, defer printing instead of using a client job to discover whether waking worked. The source tests waking but does not specify this failed-wake decision.

A designated staff member uses a maximum 60-minute after-hours session, an empty queue, the existing equipment and blank document. Do not inspect client contents or titles. If the queue cannot be cleared without touching client jobs, defer disruptive tests.

Print one blank page while awake. Leave the equipment untouched for ten minutes, then submit another. Repeat the same idle interval, this time waking both devices through ordinary controls and waiting up to two minutes for their normal ready indications before submitting. Keep settings and cable position unchanged. Reserve remaining time for separate checks: safely power down and reseat USB, then test; separately restart only the printer at its existing outlet, then test; close and reopen the blank-document application, then test. Compare individual submissions with two queued blank pages to distinguish a queue-load association from loss of device availability. Cancel only synthetic leftovers. If time expires, label uncompleted branches unresolved.

If wake-before-print helps, opening-day printing staff may adopt it provisionally at the already occurring first-print decision after a quiet period. Failure to reach readiness within two minutes triggers existing deferred-printing procedures. If readiness is ambiguous, use one blank preflight page before submitting a client job; failure ends printing attempts. Do not repeatedly resend an uncertain job. Leave the routine, stop condition and unresolved causes with the person responsible for printing; absent an accepted handoff, retain the ordinary deferral fallback. Compared with the source, this costs up to two minutes plus an occasional blank sheet but avoids relying on a sensitive document as the readiness test. It assumes normal readiness is observable; otherwise the blank preflight is necessary.
EXPAND.experiment: Within 60 minutes, compare direct submission after ten minutes idle with waking first after ten minutes idle. Record readiness time, completed blank pages, queue clearance, power indicators and availability. Repeat the matched comparison only if the remaining diagnostic and recovery time permits. Stop for abnormal power behavior, client work or an uncleared synthetic queue. If waking fails to reach readiness, exercise the deferral decision without submitting another job. One successful pair is weak evidence; if neither condition fails, report the idle hypothesis as unresolved and avoid claiming a fix.

EXPAND.title: Bypass a suspect USB socket using an existing alternative port
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: substitute the computer's USB endpoint while retaining the same printer, cable and outlet. Prior routes retain the original socket; the task does not require that dependency. A different existing port can bypass a damaged socket or port-specific communication problem without buying hardware. This is feasible only if another accessible, compatible port exists and the already installed printer works through it without administrator rights, installation or downloads.

One designated staff member runs a maximum 50-minute after-hours session with an empty queue and blank document. Start with two individual blank pages at the original port, recording completion, timing, queue state, availability and printer power indicators. Safely power down before moving connections. First reseat the cable in the original port and repeat, so a simple reseat/restart has a comparison. Then move only the computer end to the alternative port, keeping power and safe cable routing unchanged, and repeat. Reject prompts requiring elevation or installation; return to the original port. Do not select an unfamiliar printer queue without being able to establish that it belongs to this printer through ordinary device identification.

Complete separate checks within the same session: reseat the accessible power connection at the existing outlet under matched restart conditions; compare single versus two queued blank jobs; reopen the blank-document application and repeat. If another suitable application is installed, compare it with unchanged settings. These checks distinguish power, queue and application associations from port-associated behavior, although they cannot conclusively separate cable damage, drivers and USB-controller faults.

Retain the alternative port provisionally only if it works through the existing printer setup, clears every synthetic job and permits safe cable placement. Otherwise restore the original connection. The tester owns restoration and synthetic-job cleanup until the existing printing staff accept the handoff. Opening-day staff use the recorded port only while it remains reliable; on an uncertain print, stop resubmitting and use existing deferred-printing procedures. Compared with repeated reseating, port substitution could bypass a persistent socket fault, but adds device-recognition risk and is unavailable on some computers.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare original-port baseline, original-port reseat and alternative-port trials with the same blank jobs and matched restarts. If safe and time permits, return to the original port once to see whether failure follows the port; never recreate a visibly damaged or strained connection. Record outcomes without client metadata. Stop at 50 minutes, client work, abnormal electrical behavior, an installation/elevation prompt or a synthetic job that cannot be cleared ordinarily. Failure on both ports weakens a socket-specific explanation. No alternate port, no reproduced failure or improvement equally explained by restarting leaves this mechanism unconfirmed.
